what_it_does: Processing-in-memory is the idea of placing small computing units directly inside the memory chip so that data does not have to travel all the way out to the main processor for every calculation — a big win when the bottleneck is shuttling data back and forth. The UPMEM chip is a commercially available memory chip that does exactly this: it embeds simple processors inside the memory modules. However, programming these chips efficiently today requires experts to hand-tune every operation, much like early GPU programming before high-level frameworks existed. ATiM is an automated compiler that takes high-level descriptions of mathematical operations — the kind used in AI workloads, such as the large multiply-and-add operations at the heart of neural networks — and automatically searches for the best way to split and schedule that work across the many small processors inside the UPMEM chip. The compiler accounts for the unusual layout of the chip's memory banks and generates optimized low-level code without requiring the programmer to do any of this manually.
